title: The Asymmetric Development of Remote Areas in Texas
text_snippet: The Asymmetric Development of Remote Areas in Texas ABSTRACT Drawing on the reciprocal dynamics of the growth machine framework, we test whether there was a bidirectional association between road construction and land development in remote, non‐metropolitan census tracts in Texas between 2010 and 2019, during a time when these areas experienced countering land‐use pressures from resource extraction economies, exurbanization, recreational tourism, border infrastructure projects, as well as demographic and economic contraction. Furthermore, we leverage the notion of asymmetry to assess whether these countering pressures shifted the balance of the feedback loop between road construction and land development. For the analysis, we utilize recently updated satellite imagery from the National Land Cover Database's Impervious Descriptor data set, which provides longitudinal information about changes in road and non‐road human built impervious surfaces. Covering the Years 2010–2019, using two waves of first‐differenced values, we estimate two types of models: cross‐lagged structural equation models and temporally lagged first‐differenced spatial regression models. title: Place Character and the Local Welfare State: Counties' Social Services and Public Provisions Across Rural and Urban Communities
text_snippet: Place Character and the Local Welfare State: Counties' Social Services and Public Provisions Across Rural and Urban Communities ABSTRACT Relatively little attention has been given to rural local governments' social safety net and public service provisions. We develop a framework to explain how the character of communities influence social and other public services provided by local governments and why rural–urban differences may exist. Theoretically, our framework links conceptualizations of place character with welfare state theory. We illustrate our framework using original primary data collected for 1086 counties spanning the USA. The character of communities varies along economic, sociopolitical, and governmental lines. These same factors influence the services that county governments provide, with results for sociopolitical factors and local government capacity tending to follow welfare state theory. title: Mapping the Gender Gap in Italian Agriculture From Plains to Peaks, 2012 and 2021
text_snippet: Mapping the Gender Gap in Italian Agriculture From Plains to Peaks, 2012 and 2021 ABSTRACT This paper examines how gender gaps in Italian agriculture changed between 2012 and 2021 and whether those changes differed across plains, hills, and mountains. We argue that gender gaps in agriculture are terrain‐conditioned: the same resources carry different value across ecological zones because physical, infrastructural, and institutional conditions interact with gendered access to land, water, and markets. Using harmonized Italian Farm Accountancy Data Network (FADN) microdata, we estimate design‐weighted indicators in constant 2021 euros for women‐ and men‐managed farms at the national level and across altimetric belts. Both groups underwent a shared process of restructuring—greater organizational formalization, lower reliance on family‐only labor, wider use of rented land, and rising capital intensity—yet these common shifts did not produce a uniform pattern of convergence. Instead, gender differences varied across terrains: women‐managed farms gained operated area in every belt but converted it into revenue and margins unevenly, most visibly in the mountains, where substantial land expansion coincided with only modest income gains and a declining irrigated share. title: “So, Why Did You Return?”: The Journey Back to the Periphery From the Perspective of Local Returnees
text_snippet: “So, Why Did You Return?”: The Journey Back to the Periphery From the Perspective of Local Returnees ABSTRACT Rural and peripheral settings are diverse and context‐dependent, yet many are shaped by varying combinations of geographic distance, population size, access to resources and opportunities, and forms of social and community connectedness. These characteristics vary across contexts and may be associated with different configurations of disadvantage, marginalization, and place‐based strengths. The current study focused on the Israeli Northern periphery, aiming to trace the journeys of those born in the periphery as they move away and then return. It explores their perspectives on living outside the periphery, their reasons for returning, and their experiences upon returning. This study employs phenomenological methods and was conducted through semi‐structured interviews with 17 local returnees. A thematic analysis identified three main categories that characterize the locals' journey outside the periphery and back: outside the periphery is perceived as both fulfilling and allowing for a recognition of the strengths of the periphery; motivations for returning, which include economic and familial considerations on a practical level, and a sense of responsibility and recognition

title: Rural Poverty and Social Stigma: Homeless in America's Dairyland
text_snippet: Rural Poverty and Social Stigma: Homeless in America's Dairyland ABSTRACT To explain the stigma around homelessness, scholars often focus on its physically visible forms in urban centers. However, in rural contexts, people experiencing homelessness are often unseen: they are doubling up with friends and family, living in vehicles or abandoned buildings, and camping in state parks. As such, rural homelessness is often referred to as “hidden.” This hiddenness makes theories built on physical visibility partial and unable to account for the stigma around homelessness in rural contexts. Based on 6 months of ethnographic fieldwork and 37 in‐depth interviews in five rural counties in Wisconsin, this paper finds that the stigmatization of homelessness in rural areas hinges on its social hypervisibility . The scarcity of social service infrastructure forces people experiencing homelessness to depend on their social ties for support, making their struggles known to others, even when they are not directly observed. title: Formal and Informal Support Structures in Rural Military Veteran Entrepreneurship: An Ecological Systems Analysis
text_snippet: Formal and Informal Support Structures in Rural Military Veteran Entrepreneurship: An Ecological Systems Analysis ABSTRACT Military veteran entrepreneurship is central to federal transition policy, yet its institutional ecosystem was built for urban, growth‐oriented firms. Designed around formal capital pipelines, credentialing infrastructure, and institutionalized networks, the programmatic model was never built for places where relationships are the primary market infrastructure. What remains unspecified is its failure architecture—how it breaks down, for whom, and why. Drawing on interviews with 27 rural veteran entrepreneurs and 8 ecosystem actors across the Midwest, we apply ecological systems theory as a generative framework across ecological levels, from which we elaborate four mechanisms. Analysis reveals how institutional failures originate and compound across levels; when and why bonding capital substitutes for failed institutional bridging; how surname operates as ascriptive market trust that military mobility disrupts; and how unconditional disability compensation functions as an income floor that preserves entrepreneurial entry. title: Unequal STEM Opportunities and Pathways of Rural Students Across Geographical Remoteness
text_snippet: Unequal STEM Opportunities and Pathways of Rural Students Across Geographical Remoteness ABSTRACT Rural students, who represent nearly one‐fifth of the U.S. student population, remain underserved in STEM education and underrepresented in postsecondary STEM degree programs. This study examines how STEM opportunities to learn, motivational beliefs, academic preparation, and college enrollment of rural students vary across geographical remoteness areas, leveraging restricted‐use data from the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 (HSLS:09) linked to the Common Core of Data (CCD). Drawing on theoretical perspectives of opportunity‐to‐learn (OTL), situated expectancy‐value theory, and spatial inequality, this study conceptualizes STEM pathways as both academic and motivational processes embedded in geographic context. Results show that rural‐fringe students have opportunities largely comparable to suburban peers, but students in rural‐distant and especially rural‐remote schools face severe inequities in access to advanced STEM coursework and extracurricular enrichment. These OTL disparities are associated with lower STEM motivation, weaker academic preparation, and lower enrollment in four‐year STEM programs. title: Labor Force Nonparticipation in Rural and Urban America: An Examination of Prime‐Working‐Age Men and Women, 2000–2024
text_snippet: Labor Force Nonparticipation in Rural and Urban America: An Examination of Prime‐Working‐Age Men and Women, 2000–2024 ABSTRACT Labor force participation is pivotal for the economic health of individuals, families, communities, and the nation. Conversely, labor force nonparticipation represents a major challenge to economic vitality. In this study, we investigate temporal trends for those not in the labor force (NILF) among prime‐working‐age (25–54) men and women during the first quarter of the 21st century, with a focus on differences between rural and urban residents. We also seek to establish whether and how the demographic, educational, and health profiles of the population account for such trends. Drawing on data from the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement from 2000 to 2024, we estimate a series of sex‐specific linear probability models predicting the probability that an individual is NILF as a function of our explanatory variables and controls. The analysis reveals two broad findings. First, among prime‐working‐age men, the probability of NILF is consistently higher in rural areas and the gap is growing. title: Unincorporated and Unequal: Housing and Environmental Inequality Among Women Farmworkers in Rural California
text_snippet: Unincorporated and Unequal: Housing and Environmental Inequality Among Women Farmworkers in Rural California ABSTRACT This study examines how intersecting inequalities based on gender, race, class, and citizenship shape the lived experiences of Mexican and Mexican American women farmworkers in California's San Joaquin Valley, focusing on municipal boundary‐making and spatial exclusion. Drawing on 35 in‐depth interviews and feminist qualitative methods, I show how residential segregation concentrates many low‐wage and immigrant workers in unincorporated communities with limited access to basic services, safe and affordable housing, reliable transportation, and clean air and water. These conditions demonstrate how legal, municipal, and geographic boundaries operate together as mechanisms of exclusion. I conceptualize these communities as internal borderlands, where structural inequalities take shape spatially and are intensified by environmental conditions. The findings highlight how these overlapping boundaries create layered vulnerabilities with implications for housing, health, and environmental justice.

title: Home Is Where the Hope Is: Indicators of Hope in a Rural Community
text_snippet: Home Is Where the Hope Is: Indicators of Hope in a Rural Community ABSTRACT Sociologists have long used a deficit view in their work. However, some sociologists have recently turned to positive emotions, such as joy and hope, to provide a more complete view of marginalized and other populations. Largely, rural sociologists have not made the turn toward positive emotions. Rural places in the Western United States have been of interest to sociologists due to historical and contemporary social, economic, and demographic change. By focusing on these changes, sociologists have often geared their research toward how rural places are struggling and the conflict among residents. I suggest that there is a more complete view of rural places that includes hope. Using data from semi‐structured interviews, a drop‐off/pickup survey, and 2 years spent living in Beaverhead County, Montana, I found that residents of Beaverhead County appear to have both collective and individual hope for the future. My research indicates that central to this hope is a shared vision for the community's future and collective engagement in creating a place that residents want to live. title: Divergent Perceptions of Dairy Farmers on the Role of Grazing in Animal Welfare and Production
text_snippet: Divergent Perceptions of Dairy Farmers on the Role of Grazing in Animal Welfare and Production ABSTRACT The modernization of dairy production, characterized by a transition to freestall barns with automatic milking systems and increasing herd sizes, has resulted in a decline in cattle grazing. The once‐traditional practice of summer grazing in Northern Europe has become a contentious topic, with the industry and public holding divergent views regarding the importance of grazing in animal welfare and the broader sustainability of the sector. Our study is based on 15 in‐depth interviews of Finnish dairy producers with tie‐stall and freestall housing, without and with grazing of varied duration. We employ the theory of planned behavior to investigate factors that contribute to the decision‐making concerning grazing practices. The discourse surrounding grazing encompasses a range of perspectives, including but not limited to animal welfare, human–animal interactions, environmental integration, and the relationships between producers, consumers, dairy companies, and government entities. title: Depopulation, Institutional Survivorship, and Racial Inequality in Rural School Closure
text_snippet: Depopulation, Institutional Survivorship, and Racial Inequality in Rural School Closure ABSTRACT School closures have become a defining feature of educational restructuring in rural America, yet little is known about how closure risks have been distributed across schools with different racial compositions over time. Using national administrative data covering more than 96,000 public schools from 1987 to 2024, this study examines how racial composition shaped the institutional survival of rural schools during a period of population decline and policy retrenchment. Drawing on discrete‐time hazard models, I show that the relationship between White enrollment proportion and closure risk is nonlinear: schools at both ends of the racial composition distribution face lower closure odds than those in the moderate integration range, a pattern consistent with the argument that racially mixed schools occupy the most institutionally precarious position in a political economy shaped by White disinvestment from integrated public institutions. title: Rural Demographic Change in the Pandemic Era
text_snippet: Rural Demographic Change in the Pandemic Era ABSTRACT This research documents nonmetropolitan demographic trends in the era of the COVID pandemic. The rural population grew between 2020 and 2025, in contrast to a population loss between 2010 and 2020. This recent population gain occurred even though rural deaths exceeded births by a substantial margin, due to increased mortality during the pandemic. Deaths exceeded births in 81% of the rural counties, the most in history. The rural population gain was fueled entirely by net migration, which more than offset the natural decline. Migration gains occurred in 65% of the rural counties, far more than in the preceding decade. Population gains were greatest in nonmetro counties adjacent to metro areas and in recreational and retirement destination counties. As the impact of the pandemic finally waned, the nonmetro population gain increased because rural deaths diminished and net migration gains were sustained.

title: Understanding Experiences of Energy Services Access in Rural Northern US Communities: A Comparative Case Study on Recognition Justice
text_snippet: Understanding Experiences of Energy Services Access in Rural Northern US Communities: A Comparative Case Study on Recognition Justice ABSTRACT This paper reports on an ongoing study of energy services in rural, northern U.S. communities. Anchored in case studies across three northern states, the research aims to understand how residents experience energy service access. These case studies were selected for their shared histories of resource extraction and inclusion of Tribal Nations within each community. Using an online survey, the study finds that residents of these rural northern communities report facing high energy burdens, with 26% of households reporting that they spend over 10% of their income on energy costs. Energy burden varies across the three case study communities in correlation with energy costs. Heating remains predominantly dependent on fossil fuels, with only 4.6% of households utilizing heat pumps, which offer a more energy‐efficient method of heat production using electricity. Cooling demand is currently being met by inefficient systems, including central and window air conditioners. Low‐income households bear a disproportionate share of these challenges, exacerbated by poor housing insulation and reports of more frequent power outages. title: Household Labor Across the Urban–Rural Divide: Gendered Patterns of Domestic Work in Canada
text_snippet: Household Labor Across the Urban–Rural Divide: Gendered Patterns of Domestic Work in Canada ABSTRACT The persistence of gendered divisions of household labor has been well documented, but comparatively little attention has been given to how these divisions vary between urban and rural contexts. Rural households are embedded in distinct social, economic, and cultural settings that may reinforce or reshape domestic arrangements. Using nationally representative data from the Canadian General Social Survey, this study examines gender differences in time spent on household chores across urban and rural areas. We distinguish between routine tasks, such as cooking and cleaning, and nonroutine tasks, such as household repairs and yard work. Findings indicate that women continue to perform substantially more unpaid labor than men regardless of place of residence. However, the gender gap is larger in rural contexts, driven by both rural men's lower engagement in routine chores and rural women's higher total time in domestic work compared to their urban counterparts. These results suggest that rural residence amplifies traditional gendered patterns of labor. title: Accumulation and Anticipation: A Temporal Reframing of Social and Cultural Capital
text_snippet: Accumulation and Anticipation: A Temporal Reframing of Social and Cultural Capital ABSTRACT This paper argues that social and cultural capital are not only accumulations of past ties, credentials, and dispositions but also temporally oriented resources aligned with anticipated futures. Although capital is theorized as generative and field‐dependent, empirical measures typically operationalize it retrospectively, tracking established networks and recognized identities rather than actors' positioning amid emerging social, economic, and ecological change. I introduce the concept of anticipatory capital to capture these temporal alignments, distinguishing between capital that reinforces inherited pathways and capital that repositions actors toward evolving fields. Integrating this perspective clarifies why individuals, households, and communities with comparable capital stocks experience divergent outcomes during periods of rapid transition. By making temporal alignment explicit, anticipatory capital clarifies how social and cultural assets fluctuate in value as fields evolve, sharpening analyses of inequality, resilience, and vulnerability and offering a framework for assessing how communities prepare for—or resist—structural transformation.

title: Natural Climate Solutions, Indigenous Peoples, Mestizos, and the Legacies of Conflict Over Land in the Ecuadorian Amazon
text_snippet: Natural Climate Solutions, Indigenous Peoples, Mestizos, and the Legacies of Conflict Over Land in the Ecuadorian Amazon ABSTRACT Over the past two decades as global alarm over disruptive climate change has grown, coalitions of high‐ranking government officials and prominent activists have launched campaigns to protect and restore greenhouse gas absorbing rain forests. The initial results from these campaigns have varied dramatically across racial and ethnic landholding groups. A case study of environmental initiatives in the Ecuadorian Amazon, presented here, begins to explain these patterns in the adoption of natural climate solutions. Indigenous peoples, practicing a kind of defensive environmentalism, have been effective at protecting the old growth tropical rain forests that they inhabit. Their ability to mobilize and defend forests stems from earlier conflicts with settler colonists in which indigenous groups defended their access to forests from incursions by settlers. When settlers occupied the land, they initially destroyed forests, only to later foster the regrowth of trees in actively managed pastures.

title: Coastal Farmers' and Agricultural Landowners' Perceptions of Marsh Migration and Emerging Socio‐Ecological Vulnerabilities Related to Sea‐Level Rise
text_snippet: Coastal Farmers' and Agricultural Landowners' Perceptions of Marsh Migration and Emerging Socio‐Ecological Vulnerabilities Related to Sea‐Level Rise ABSTRACT Sea‐level rise (SLR) has the potential to profoundly impact coastal ecosystems and human communities. SLR will cause marshes to erode on their seaward edge, but marsh migration onto uplands may allow for their persistence and continued provision of ecosystem services. Low elevation agricultural land may be well‐suited for marsh migration; however, SLR and associated marsh migration on agricultural land could negatively impact farmers and landowners, underscoring the value of exploring both social and ecological dimensions of marsh migration. We conducted semi‐structured interviews ( n = 12) with coastal farmers and agricultural landowners on the Eastern Shore of Virginia, USA to understand their experiences with and perceptions of impacts of marsh migration on their agricultural lands and in their community. While interviewees acknowledged some benefits of marsh migration, the preservation of farmland was preferred over allowing marsh migration. title: America's Empty Homes: The Overlooked Rural and Nonmetropolitan Housing Vacancy Problem
text_snippet: America's Empty Homes: The Overlooked Rural and Nonmetropolitan Housing Vacancy Problem ABSTRACT This study examines structural housing vacancy as an underrecognized dimension of rural and nonmetropolitan inequality in the United States. Rural areas experiencing structural vacancy face economic strain, weakened housing markets, fiscal stress, and cycles of disinvestment and population loss. Existing research emphasizes metropolitan contexts and absolute vacancy counts, obscuring rural and nonmetropolitan patterns that become visible when vacancy is measured as a percentage of total housing units and when seasonal housing is analytically separated. Using county‐level data from the 2015–2019 American Community Survey, this study examines the correlates of structural housing vacancy—defined as vacant housing units excluding those used for seasonal, recreational, or occasional purposes. Results indicate that structural vacancy is strongly associated with economic disadvantage, weaker housing markets, rural remoteness, and regional context. In contrast, seasonal vacancy reflects amenity‐driven dynamics tied to aging populations, retirement migration, and second‐home ownership. title: Community in Context: The Effect of the Local Community on the Experience of Community
text_snippet: Community in Context: The Effect of the Local Community on the Experience of Community ABSTRACT To what extent does community context shape individuals' experience of community? This study replicates and extends Flaherty and Brown's multilevel application of Kasarda and Janowitz’ systemic model using four separate multilevel datasets and multiple measures of community experience. The results reaffirm Flaherty and Brown's findings and support the systemic model by showing that community attachment varies little across communities and is primarily explained by individual‐level variables. In contrast, psychological sense of community appears to vary more substantially between communities and may provide a more nuanced and effective way to assess community experience. The authors urge community sociologists to reflect on the original rationale for using community attachment and to consider the theoretical implications of its limited variance between communities—despite its longstanding use as a key community‐level social indicator.

title: When Vulnerability Is Mistaken for Justice: Just Readiness and the Political Grammars of Colorado's Coal Transition
text_snippet: When Vulnerability Is Mistaken for Justice: Just Readiness and the Political Grammars of Colorado's Coal Transition ABSTRACT This paper examines how “community readiness” operates within just transition governance, arguing that readiness frameworks—though intended to support locally grounded, participatory change—can also unevenly shape recognition, participation, and repair. In rural transition contexts, readiness is often treated as evidence of legitimacy and fairness through cohesion, consensus, and institutional alignment—even as these qualities may obscure internal inequalities and foreclose contested futures. Drawing on postcolonial feminist theory, recognition justice, and scholarship on anticipatory governance, the paper reconceptualizes readiness not as a neutral measure of capacity but as a governing grammar that organizes who counts as the community, how disagreement is interpreted, and which futures are rendered actionable. Empirically, the paper analyzes Colorado's effort to decarbonize its electricity system by 2040, focusing on the institutional architecture created to manage coal plant closures and support coal‐dependent regions. title: Community as Story: Identity, Place, and Narrative in San Juan County, Utah, USA
text_snippet: Community as Story: Identity, Place, and Narrative in San Juan County, Utah, USA ABSTRACT Existing research demonstrates strong connections between community, identity, place, and narrative. Using a case study focused on the Bears Ears National Monument in San Juan County, Utah, USA, this paper utilizes the framework of “community as story” to explore how narratives both draw on and shape local identity. Through an exploratory content analysis of publicly available media, we examine how residents responded to changes in their communities. Locals expressed their connection to the land through personal and collective narratives, often invoking family history, stewardship, and memories tied to place. Our findings illustrate that residents use storytelling not only to affirm their individual and collective identities but also to resist perceived threats to their community. By demonstrating how place‐based narratives influence community responses to change, this study advances our understanding of the relational dimensions of community and underscores the importance of local voices in discussions on land use and policy.

title: Farmers' Perspectives on Participatory Breeding of Native Maize in Mexico: A Rural Application to Q‐Methodology
text_snippet: Farmers' Perspectives on Participatory Breeding of Native Maize in Mexico: A Rural Application to Q‐Methodology ABSTRACT Although numerous farmer innovation strategies have been proposed to address the challenges in rural areas, there remains limited knowledge about how to effectively facilitate their adoption. This study utilizes Q‐methodology to identify the key factors influencing the adoption of a participatory breeding strategy for native maize in the central region of Veracruz, Mexico. The methodology was applied with 16 farmers, revealing three distinct perspectives regarding the most viable ways to promote this strategy: (1) fostering government intervention to provide resources and technical support, (2) ensuring the strategy results in increased economic benefits for families, and (3) prioritizing collective work and achieving prompt, tangible outcomes. The study highlights the importance of understanding the diversity of expectations among farmers regarding agricultural innovation strategies promoted by research groups, governmental institutions, and NGOs. Far from being homogenous, these expectations reflect complex and, at times, conflicting perspectives, underscoring the need for tailored approaches that consider local priorities and dynamics.

title: Measuring Perceptions of Rural America: An Integration of Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis
text_snippet: Measuring Perceptions of Rural America: An Integration of Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis ABSTRACT The purpose of this study was to develop and validate the first instrument specifically designed to measure public perceptions of rural America. The researcher‐developed instrument was comprised of 22 items. An exploratory factor analysis and a confirmatory factor analysis were conducted in two different samples: a group of undergraduate students and a national sample. A four‐factor model of the scale was confirmed, including community strengths and safety, economic and educational challenges, health and addiction issues, and social discrimination and cultural tensions. The scale is appropriate for measuring perceptions of rural Americans reliably and accurately. A better understanding of the perceptions of rural America will help educators and communicators identify and promote solutions for the issues and challenges facing those communities.

title: Is Rural America Older Than Urban America? The Answer Depends on the Decade
text_snippet: Is Rural America Older Than Urban America? The Answer Depends on the Decade ABSTRACT Residents of rural America being older than urban residents is often viewed as a fundamental demographic difference between these two populations, with rural population aging seen as both a cause and consequence of economic and epidemiological hardships found in rural communities. However, it is currently unknown how historically rooted this demographic divide is and if it will persist in the future. This study asks one descriptive question: how has the age structure of rural and urban populations changed—or will change—between 1920 and 2060? Historical full count microdata, county‐level population counts, and multiple population projections are used to estimate the median age of rural and urban residents. From 1920 to 1960 individuals living in counties currently classified as rural were unexpectedly younger than their urban peers. Although rural populations were older from 1970 to 2020 and are likely to remain so in the near future, population projections suggest that urban median ages will catch up by 2060. title: Landowner Perspectives on Large‐Scale Solar Leasing: Decision‐Making and Agricultural Implications in Rural New York State
text_snippet: Landowner Perspectives on Large‐Scale Solar Leasing: Decision‐Making and Agricultural Implications in Rural New York State ABSTRACT As the decarbonization‐driven energy transition accelerates, land‐intensive renewable energy technologies, and large‐scale solar facilities (LSS) in particular, increasingly compete for rural land. In the Northeast United States, LSS development largely depends on private landowners' decisions to lease land for LSS development. Little research has documented the characteristics of landowners who either agree or refuse to contract with LSS developers nor how they are likely to change their future land management, especially agricultural practices. Drawing on a survey of 1499 rural landowners ( n = 584 responses) conducted in three counties of New York State, currently ranked 8th nationally in solar energy production, but with even more ambitious solar production goals, this study explores landowner beliefs, decision‐making, and intended land management behavior concerning LSS development. Nearly half of respondents had been approached to lease land for LSS development. title: On Repeat? The Logic of Agricultural Modernization, the Choices of Tanzanian Small‐Scale Farmers, and Implications for the Second Green Revolution
text_snippet: On Repeat? The Logic of Agricultural Modernization, the Choices of Tanzanian Small‐Scale Farmers, and Implications for the Second Green Revolution ABSTRACT The Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) is the latest in a series of initiatives aimed at modernizing small‐scale farming to address food insecurity and poverty, yet AGRA has fallen short of its goals. This study explores whether these shortcomings might stem from flawed assumptions in AGRA's theory of change—assumptions long embedded in top‐down agricultural modernization efforts. We situate AGRA within broader debates on the agrarian question, especially the Chayanov–Lenin debate, and draw historical parallels with United States agricultural industrialization, the Green Revolution, and Soviet collectivization, as well as Tanzania's villagization program. Tanzania is an instructive case, having undergone both collectivist and market‐based modernization. Using Chayanov's theory of peasant household decision‐making, we analyze panel survey data from the Tanzania National Panel Survey (TNPS), part of the World Bank Living Standards Measurement Study—Integrated Surveys on Agriculture (LSMS‐ISA) program, to examine how household demographic factors relate to labor and land use decisions. title: Beyond “Deaths of Despair”: Narratives of Distress and Risk‐Taking Behaviors Among Rural Working‐Class Men
text_snippet: Beyond “Deaths of Despair”: Narratives of Distress and Risk‐Taking Behaviors Among Rural Working‐Class Men ABSTRACT White working‐class men living in rural areas are affected by increased rates of distress thought to lead to risk‐taking behaviors. This study advances understanding of risk‐taking‐related distress by examining how men interpret their experiences and how these meaning‐making processes connect to shifting social‐structural conditions in rural working‐class life. Drawing on 14 interviews with men affected by risk‐taking‐related distress, I find that men's descriptions largely focus on interpersonal relationships and often center on the end of romantic relationships with women, which they describe as unfair or undeserved. When respondents describe internal states, they report feeling depressed and having nothing and display feelings of resentment. Findings suggest that this group's declining social position has led to a mismatch between expectations and resources necessary for achieving those expectations. A sense of failing to meet directives of their working‐class masculine identities—especially maintaining control in heterosexual romantic relationships—may lead men to manage distress by engaging in risk‐taking behavior. title: Conditions of Possibility for Deep Social Change—Imaginaries Concerning Normality in a Finnish Online Discussion on Self‐Sufficiency
text_snippet: Conditions of Possibility for Deep Social Change—Imaginaries Concerning Normality in a Finnish Online Discussion on Self‐Sufficiency ABSTRACT As part of the literature that emphasizes alternative narratives as a prominent means of promoting change in the face of the climate crisis and other ecological catastrophes, we concentrate on local self‐sufficiency, which has been identified as one of the promising paths to sustainability. Inductive content analysis of public discussion of radical self‐sufficiency on a Finnish newspaper website, using two sets of data 10 years apart, uncovered shared features in people's evaluation and reasoning on self‐sufficiency. From the discussion, a social imaginary of a desirable “normal” state, characterized in terms of the monetary economy and technological progress, is readily identifiable. In contrast, change toward a self‐sufficient lifestyle is seen as contingent on several factors: it being universalizable, contributing to common goals, and discouraging living off other people. These findings suggest that efforts to articulate narratives of low natural resource use must pay heed to broadening the social imagination, while simultaneously highlighting opportunities to participate meaningfully in society.

title: The Farm Workforce Modernization Act: Finding Common Ground at the Crossroads of Immigration and Labor Policy
text_snippet: The Farm Workforce Modernization Act: Finding Common Ground at the Crossroads of Immigration and Labor Policy ABSTRACT This case study of the 2019 Farm Workforce Modernization Act explains how immigration policy is framed and how compromise is generated among legislators and interest groups with conflicting goals. This research relies on a content analysis of publicly available primary documents dating from 2019 to 2020, and a qualitative survey of 20 farmworker advocates. We argue that three overarching frames defined the policy problem and thus shaped policy proposals: (1) exploitative working conditions, (2) access to cheap labor, and (3) the rule of law. Further, we identified emotional appeals that buttressed each frame, consisting of ethics, agricultural exceptionalism, and the undeserving/deserving binary. Our analysis also reveals the Faustian bargains of members of the policy network and opposition from groups in the wider policy community. title: A Not‐So‐Just Transition? Examining the Effects of Coal Sector Decline on Life Expectancy in U.S. Counties
text_snippet: A Not‐So‐Just Transition? Examining the Effects of Coal Sector Decline on Life Expectancy in U.S. Counties ABSTRACT Driven by climate and energy policy priorities in national and global contexts, coal phase‐out is expected to improve public health outcomes by reducing human exposure to air, water, and soil pollution and decreasing the number of workers in dangerous mining conditions. However, the transition may also increase economic distress in mining communities leading to poorer health outcomes—possibly offsetting the benefits of phasing out coal. We examine this hypothesis by assessing the relation between coal production, working hours per miner, coal mining employment, and life expectancy in 3076 U.S. counties (97.9% of all U.S. counties) from 2012 to 2019. We develop and apply a novel spatial modeling approach that combines the high‐dimensional half‐panel jackknife fixed effects estimator with the spatial lag of X model and examine whether increases and decreases in each predictor are associated with life expectancy.
